title: Group Velocity in Waves and Oscillations
short_intro: Group velocity is the velocity with which the overall shape of the amplitudes of a wave packet—known as the envelope—propagates through space. It represents the speed at which wave energy and information are transmitted in a dispersive medium.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of phase and group velocity, formula derivation for non-dispersive media where v_g = v_p, and simple numerical problems involving wave number and angular frequency.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced relationship between group velocity and phase velocity in dispersive media, expression involving wavelength (v_g = v_p - lambda \frac{dv_p}{dlambda}), relation with refractive index, and wave packet spreading.

prerequisites: Simple Harmonic Motion and Wave Equation
Superposition Principle of Waves and Beats

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance
bullets: Group velocity is defined as the velocity of the envelope of a wave packet formed by the superposition of two or more waves of slightly different frequencies.
It represents the speed of energy propagation, whereas phase velocity represents the speed of individual phase fronts.
In a non-dispersive medium, all frequency components travel at the same speed, making the group velocity equal to the phase velocity.

concept_notes.heading: Dispersive vs Non-Dispersive Media
bullets: A medium is termed dispersive if the phase velocity depends on the frequency or wavelength of the wave.
In normal dispersion, phase velocity increases with wavelength (dv_p/dlambda < 0), causing group velocity to be less than phase velocity (v_g < v_p).
In anomalous dispersion, phase velocity decreases with wavelength (dv_p/dlambda > 0), leading to a group velocity greater than phase velocity (v_g > v_p).

concept_notes.heading: Mathematical Formulation
bullets: Expressed mathematically as v_g = domega/dk, where omega is the angular frequency and k is the angular wave number.
Relates to phase velocity v_p = omega/k via the differential operation.
For electromagnetic waves in an ionosphere or plasma, the product of group velocity and phase velocity is constant: v_g v_p = c^2.

concept_notes.heading: Wave Packet and Dispersion
bullets: A localized wave packet is constructed using Fourier components spanning a small range of wave numbers Delta k.
Due to different frequency components traveling at different velocities in a dispersive medium, the wave packet broadens or spreads out over time.
The spatial width of the wave packet is inversely proportional to the spread in wave number, satisfying the uncertainty principle Delta x Delta k ge 1/2.

derivations.title: Relation between Group Velocity and Phase Velocity
derivations.conditions: Superposition of two waves of equal amplitude, slightly differing frequencies (omega, omega + domega) and wave numbers (k, k + dk).
steps: Write the displacement equations for the two interfering waves: y_1 = a cos(omega t - kx) and y_2 = a cos((omega + domega)t - (k + dk)x).
Apply the superposition principle y = y_1 + y_2 and use the trigonometric identity for the sum of cosines.
The resulting displacement is given by y = 2a cosleft(\frac{domega}{2} t - \frac{dk}{2} x\right) cos(omega t - kx).
Identify the envelope term traveling at group velocity v_g = \frac{domega}{dk} and the carrier wave term traveling at phase velocity v_p = \frac{omega}{k}.

derivations.title: Alternative Expression for Group Velocity in Terms of Wavelength
derivations.conditions: Wave propagation in a dispersive medium where phase velocity depends on wavelength lambda.
steps: Start from the fundamental definition of group velocity in terms of angular frequency and wave number: v_g = \frac{domega}{dk}.
Express angular frequency as omega = k v_p, where v_p is a function of k.
Differentiate with respect to k: v_g = \frac{d}{dk}(kv_p) = v_p + k \frac{dv_p}{dk}.

Substitute the relation between wave number and wavelength, k = \frac{2pi}{lambda}, and apply the chain rule: \frac{dv_p}{dk} = \frac{dv_p}{dlambda} \frac{dlambda}{dk} = -\frac{lambda^2}{2pi} \frac{dv_p}{dlambda}.
Substitute back to obtain the final expression: v_g = v_p - lambda \frac{dv_p}{dlambda}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Formation of a Wave Packet (Envelope and Carrier)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A high-frequency sinusoidal carrier wave modulated by a slower, broader envelope curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how localized wave packets are formed by constructive and destructive interference of neighboring frequencies.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Visual identification of phase velocity (speed of inner crests) vs group velocity (speed of envelope peak).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Dispersion Curve (omega vs k)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A non-linear curve of angular frequency omega plotted against wave number k, with a tangent line drawn at a specific point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the tangent at any point gives the group velocity (v_g = domega/dk), while the slope of the secant line from the origin gives the phase velocity (v_p = omega/k).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Graphical determination of v_g and v_p to classify media as normal or anomalous.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wave Packet Spreading in a Dispersive Medium
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A series of wave packet amplitude profiles at successive time intervals t_1, t_2, t_3 showing both translation and horizontal broadening.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that different frequency components travel at different speeds, causing the pulse to lose its sharpness over distance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining limitations in signal transmission and communication channel bandwidth.

solved_numericals.question: If the angular frequency of a wave is given by omega = 5k^2 + 2k, find the group velocity at wave number k = 2 rad/m.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for group velocity: v_g = \frac{domega}{dk}.
Differentiate the given dispersion relation omega = 5k^2 + 2k with respect to k: \frac{domega}{dk} = 10k + 2.
Substitute the given value k = 2 into the derivative: v_g = 10(2) + 2 = 20 + 2 = 22 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: For deep water gravity waves, the phase velocity is given by v_p = sqrt{\frac{glambda}{2pi}}. Calculate the group velocity of these waves.
solution_steps: Use the relation between group velocity and phase velocity: v_g = v_p - lambda \frac{dv_p}{dlambda}.

Find the derivative of phase velocity with respect to wavelength: \frac{dv_p}{dlambda} = \frac{d}{dlambda}left(left(\frac{g}{2pi}\right)^{1/2} lambda^{1/2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} left(\frac{g}{2pi}\right)^{1/2} lambda^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2lambda} sqrt{\frac{glambda}{2pi}} = \frac{v_p}{2lambda}.
Substitute the derivative back into the formula: v_g = v_p - lambda left(\frac{v_p}{2lambda}\right) = v_p - \frac{v_p}{2} = \frac{1}{2} v_p.

solved_numericals.question: A medium has a dispersion relation omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_p^2, where c and omega_p are constants. Find the product of group velocity and phase velocity.
solution_steps: Find group velocity by differentiating omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_p^2 implicitly with respect to k: 2omega \frac{domega}{dk} = 2c^2 k implies v_g = \frac{domega}{dk} = \frac{c^2 k}{omega}.
Calculate the product v_g v_p: v_g v_p = left(\frac{c^2 k}{omega}\right) left(\frac{omega}{k}\right) = c^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the wave packet is formed by a narrow band of frequencies, so that dispersion across the band is negligible.
Does not account for severe attenuation or absorption in the medium, which would alter the amplitude envelope independently of dispersion.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Group velocity is always greater than or equal to phase velocity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Group velocity can be less than, greater than, or equal to phase velocity depending on whether the dispersion is normal or anomalous.
common_misconceptions.why: In normal dispersion, dv_p/dlambda < 0 makes v_g < v_p.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Phase velocity can never exceed the speed of light in a vacuum.
common_misconceptions.correct: Phase velocity can exceed c (e.g., in wave guides or anomalous dispersion regions), but group velocity (representing energy flow) never exceeds c.
common_misconceptions.why: Phase velocity does not transmit physical signals or energy, whereas group velocity does.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Group velocity and phase velocity are identical for all mechanical waves.
common_misconceptions.correct: They are identical only in non-dispersive media (like sound waves in air at constant temperature); most physical media are dispersive.
common_misconceptions.why: Frequency dependence of wave speed inherently separates group and phase velocities.

quick_revision: Group velocity represents the speed of energy transmission and is given by v_g = domega/dk.
In a dispersive medium with normal dispersion, v_g < v_p.
For deep water gravity waves, group velocity is half of phase velocity.
In waveguides or plasma, the product of group and phase velocities equals the square of the speed of light in a vacuum (v_g v_p = c^2).
